entry.title: Hold the practice lesson at ten questions
entry.content:
Hold the practice lesson at ten questions

The session was already built for ten. It padded to ten *rows* and then
dropped every row the card loop could not turn into a question — a word
with no translation, or too few distinct distractors — so a queue with
seven unusable words produced a three-card lesson. Rows are not cards,
and nothing in the code had noticed the difference.

Two changes, and the cheap one does most of the work.

A word that fails the translation MCQ now gets asked its meaning instead
of being dropped. A definition card needs no translation at all, so the
words the translation path cannot use are often perfectly askable, and
the pool it draws on is already built for the every-fourth-card slot.
That costs nothing and converts most drops into questions.

Rows are also over-provisioned by four, and the loop stops once it has
SESSION_SIZE cards. Deliberately four rather than double: every extra
row is a lemma through the translation batch and a padded lemma is
usually a cache miss on a paid API. It is a margin against a near-zero
drop rate, not against a broken one — which is why the rescue above had
to come first.

The definition card is now built once per row and used in either place
it is wanted, rather than from a closure over the loop variable. Same
behaviour, and it does not depend on a closure that is a lint error
today and a real footgun the day someone defers it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Give definition cards a fallback, and the edges real thickness
entry.content:
Give definition cards a fallback, and the edges real thickness

Two faults from the last change, and the first is why no definition card
ever appeared.

`build_definition_choices` had no fallback. `build_translation_choices`
has always dropped back to the deck's own translations when the outside
pool is thin, so a cold pool costs it variety; this returned None
instead, and the caller quietly reverted to a translation card. A pool
that comes back empty — a registry bucket with no (pos, level) match, a
lemma the registry has no part of speech for — therefore turned the
whole feature off rather than degrading it, and it did so silently on
every card.

It now falls back to the session's own other words. They are weaker
distractors, since a deck word may be an answer later in the same
session, but they are level-appropriate by construction, and a slightly
weaker question beats no question at all. The pool is still preferred
outright; the deck only tops up a shortfall. A fallback that also comes
up short still returns None, and that case now logs which slot it lost
so it is visible rather than inferred.

The edges were lines because a 4pt box with a 14pt corner radius is not
a thin slab — the radius eats the whole shape, leaving nothing with any
thickness to see. They are full-height copies of the tile offset down
now, exactly as the word deck's pills are: top EDGE, bottom 0, height
never set so a long option's edge grows with it. Only the face moves on
press, so the visible band shrinks rather than the whole tile sliding.
Same for the CTA, whose strip was 5pt under a 16pt radius.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Ask the definition every fourth card, on one flat surface
entry.content:
Ask the definition every fourth card, on one flat surface

Every fourth card now asks which word means a gloss, instead of which
translation belongs to a word. Same grid, same scoring, same boolean
posted — only the question changes, so nothing downstream of the tap had
to learn a new shape.

Distractors come from a second pool of English lemmas, matched on part
of speech and CEFR level the way the translation pool already is. That
is what keeps them from being *too remote*: a B2 verb among B2 verbs is
a question about meaning, while the same verb among A1 nouns is a
question about grammar that answers itself. `is_near_form` does the
other half — a definition for "console" with "consoled" beside it is not
harder, it is unfair, and a registry bucket is full of morphological
neighbours. `avoid` carries the words already spent this session, which
is the *too repetitive* half. Falling short of three usable distractors
returns None and the card reverts to its translation MCQ rather than
being dropped.

The lemma pool is the cheaper of the two: no translation cache to read
and nothing discarded for want of a cached entry, so it is as wide on a
cold language as on a warm one.

On the card, the word is blanked out of the example sentence rather than
highlighted in it. The sentence is the second half of the question;
lighting the word up would print the answer directly above the options.

The backdrop is flat now — the same `background` the practice path uses.
The tinted vignette was three stacked gradients standing in for a radial
one, and it began directly under the progress panel, so the two read as
two surfaces with a seam between them. A gradient that ends is a line.
The footer's own fade and hairline went for the same reason.

Options and the CTA are the word deck's buttons: paper face, 1.5pt rim,
solid edge beneath. Both take the verdict's colours, which they now have
to — the backdrop is no longer saying it behind them. The two-stop
gradient fill and the soft ambient shadow went with it; a solid edge and
a blurred drop are two ways of saying the same tile is raised.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Round the practice tile, drop its ring, crack the floor on tap
entry.content:
Round the practice tile, drop its ring, crack the floor on tap

The tile is a circle. 72x56 was the footprint of an ellipse drawn "seen
slightly from above"; once the ellipse went, the stadium left behind was
wider than tall for a reason that no longer existed.

The turning ring of dots is gone, and TileRing with it. The bounce
already marks the one tappable tile, and a second permanent animation on
the same object was two things competing to say one thing.

Tapping now lands the tile. The bounce stops where it is and does not
restart for that mount — a tap is a commitment, and a tile that keeps
hovering after you have chosen it is still asking to be chosen — the
face sinks onto its edge, and a fan of fissures spreads from underneath.

TileCrack draws them, rendered before the coin and anchored to its
baseline, so the tile's own body covers every line's origin and only
what escapes the silhouette shows. That is what makes them read as
coming out from under the tile rather than lying beside it. It fires on
press-in rather than press: `onPress` lands on release, by which time
the navigation this tile starts is already under way and there is
nothing left to watch.

The ink is `text` at low alpha rather than a fixed dark. On light that
is a dark crack in a pale floor; on dark it inverts to a lit fissure,
which is the same idea and the only version visible at all on a
near-black ground.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Rebuild the practice tile on the deck buttons' construction
entry.content:
Rebuild the practice tile on the deck buttons' construction

The cave was the ellipse. An ellipse narrows to a point at its left and
right extremes, so near those points the face occupies a sliver of
height around its own centre line and the edge occupies one around a
centre line 8pt lower — the two stop overlapping and the background
shows through between them. It read as a hollow under each side rather
than as thickness.

A capsule cannot do that. Its radius is half its height, so an offset
copy still overlaps everywhere and the only thing visible beneath the
face is an even band, which is what the illusion needs and all it needs.
That is why the word deck's pills never had the problem, and the tile is
now built the same way: a face, a darker copy of it offset down, and the
face alone sinking on press.

Four effects went with the ellipse — a gradient across the face, a white
rim fading out by the equator, a specular oval, and a second gradient on
the edge. They were doing the work the offset already does, and each was
a place for the two shapes to disagree. `matte` went with them, since it
existed only to switch the gloss and the rim off for locked tiles.

Being two plain views rather than an SVG root also costs a dozen fewer
SVG roots on a full path. The alarm glyph keeps its own small Svg and
rides inside the face, so it still sinks on press without a transform.

entry.title: Step back one card at a time, all the way to the first
entry.content:
Step back one card at a time, all the way to the first

I read the last request as "jump to card 1" and it was "keep working
until card 1". The button moves one card per press again — but off the
deck's own order rather than a stack of cards this session happened to
advance past, which is what was broken in the first place. Open a film
at card 11 because the bookmark put you there and that stack is empty,
so the button could not reach cards 1 to 10 at all. It stopped exactly
where you had been dropped, which is the one place a "back" control has
no reason to respect.

The bookmark moves with each step, so leaving and returning resumes
where the stepping left off instead of snapping forward again.

It is flat now. The pills are raised because they are the decision; this
is the way back from it, and a third control with the same 3D lift made
the row read as three equal buttons rather than a choice with an escape
beside it. The press reads as a dim instead of a drop, and UNDO_EDGE is
gone — the row's height was always the pill's, so nothing moves.

Next gets the rim "Knew it" wears, in the colour of its own edge layer:
outlined by the shade it sits on rather than by a fourth gold nobody
chose, and it stops a solid gold button dissolving into the paper on a
light ground.

entry.title: Five deck and hero tweaks
entry.content:
Five deck and hero tweaks

The backdrop comes forward, 0.24 to 0.42. Every layer over it stays —
the gold tint, the fade into the page — and only more of the photograph
comes through them. Held that far back it had stopped being a grade and
become a lid, and the film still has to be recognisable for the deck
being the subject to read as a choice rather than an absence.

The circular button restarts the deck instead of stepping back one card.
The deck already restores you to a bookmark on every open, so "where you
left off" is a place the app puts you rather than one you chose, and the
control people reached for was the one that got them out of it. Twenty
presses to reach the top is a chore. It rewrites the bookmark from card
one so the restart survives the next visit, and the undo stack it used
to walk is gone.

Next's label is white in light mode. It measures 2.96:1 on that theme's
#C58B1B — just under what 14pt/900 would want, and chosen deliberately
after seeing the number. Dark mode keeps the dark ink: white there is
1.36:1 on #FFD166, which is not a trade-off, it is invisible.

The save heart goes 21 to 25, from one constant so both card faces
measure the same and it cannot jump as the fly-away overlay detaches.

"Knew it" now reports itself through the global toast, with its Undo,
exactly as the film feed's "Seen it" and "Not interested" do. This
screen had grown a bespoke bar with its own view, styles and dismissal,
so the app answered you in two different places depending on where you
were standing. The toast's dwell is the commit window rather than the
default 3.6s — held apart, the gap between them is a window with nothing
on screen to press and still time to press it. It also says what
happened; the old bar said `"word" hidden`, which described a row
leaving a list this screen no longer shows.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: "Knew it", in the app's own accent
entry.content:
"Knew it", in the app's own accent

Past tense, because the button is a report rather than a claim: you are
telling the deck you already had this word, not asserting that you know
it now. Its screen-reader label follows.

The green is gone. `tc.success` is not unused — but everywhere else it
appears it means *correct*: a right MCQ answer, a finished session's
tick, the quiz backdrop, the "Seen it" swipe. Dismissing a word you
already knew is not a correctness judgement, so borrowing that colour
put a verdict on a button that was only ever a filter, and it was the
one green on a screen made of gold and paper.

The three controls under the deck are now one family in the one accent,
separated by weight rather than hue: Next is filled gold, "Knew it" is
a strong outline in the readable-on-paper gold, Undo is a hairline.
That is the same primary/secondary pairing every sheet uses, and it is
why both pills now share `nodeGoldEdge` for the 3D edge under them.

Only the English string changed. The other five locales still translate
the present tense, and two of them ("Bunu bilin", "Saiba disso") are
imperatives that were wrong before this — worth a pass, but not one to
guess at five languages deep.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Let the scaled deck reach the film edge on Android
entry.content:
Let the scaled deck reach the film edge on Android

The card still sat well inside the sprocket strips on an S24, and the
reason was the floor I put under the last fix. The exact compensation
there is about 4pt; a floor of 8 raised it, pushing the card further in
than the solve had asked for. The only real constraint is that the box
must not exceed its parent — 0 guarantees that, and 8 was caution with
no failure behind it.

The inset is now solved against a target rendered position rather than a
target width, which is the thing that can actually be pointed at on a
screenshot:

    rendered inset = m + (width - 2m)(1 - scale) / 2

Android aims at 14, where the film-edge sprockets are (FilmEdgeBackdrop
draws them at left 6, width 8) — the card may reach them and must not
cross them. iOS keeps 18 and its floor, because that is what has been
looked at on a device and signed off; the maths is the same and only the
two numbers differ, so it stays one function with one test rather than a
platform branch in the layout.

Below roughly 0.92 on a 360pt screen the target stops being reachable —
the solve wants a negative margin — so it gives everything it has and
the card is as wide as it can be. My first draft of the test asserted
the target was always hit and failed on correct code for that reason.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Give Android the deck's full width and a gap above the tab bar
entry.content:
Give Android the deck's full width and a gap above the tab bar

Two Android faults, two causes.

The deck was narrower because the scale is uniform. It exists to fit the
card *vertically* — the slots are fixed heights, so a short viewport
shrinks the zone rather than re-cutting it — but `transform: scale`
takes the sides with it, and a Samsung S24 is shorter than an iPhone
without being short of width. The result was a scaled-down card with
unused gutters either side of it.

The side inset now gives back exactly what the scale took: widen the
pre-transform box by 1/scale and the transform returns the card to the
width an unscaled one would have had. The extra design width inside is
spent on the type and then scaled back, so the card reads at the same
size in space that was already there. Floored at 8pt, because the exact
compensation goes negative under a hard enough squeeze and a child laid
out wider than its parent stops receiving touches on Android — the card
would look right and answer nothing.

The missing gap was simpler and worse. The floating capsule reserves its
height plus TOP_GAP; the pinned bar reserved its height and nothing else,
so content stopped flush against it. On Android that is the deck's
controls resting on the tab bar with the system's own navigation
directly below — three rows of controls with no separation anywhere.
iOS never showed it because the capsule is inset from the screen edge
anyway, so the gap was there by accident there and missing by accident
everywhere else. Both shapes reserve the same clearance now.

Two tests asserted `reservedHeight === barHeight` for the pinned bar.
They were pinning the bug, so they are rewritten rather than relaxed —
"flush" describes where the bar sits, not how close content may come.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Redesign the hero line and the deck's three controls
entry.content:
Redesign the hero line and the deck's three controls

The film's band and its match rate were one mono line reading "C1 72%",
which made a level and a rate look like a single value. They are now a
chip and a figure, and they sit ABOVE the title — the word feed's card
and the deck's card both lead with the level and then give the subject,
so the screen's header finally reads the same way as the things inside
it. The chip takes its colour from the shared ramp, so a level is one
colour everywhere on the screen; the percentage deliberately does not,
because it is a fact about the reader rather than about the film and
one colour for both would fold two measurements into one mark.

The two pills lose their glyphs. A tick beside "I know it" and an arrow
beside "Next" each said the label a second time, and two words read
quicker than a word plus a symbol.

Colours come off tokens now. Next is flat `tc.gold` on `tc.goldDeep` —
the same fill and ink every sheet's Done wears, where it used to be a
two-stop gradient of four frozen hexes and the only gradient in the app,
which made the deck's main action look like it came from somewhere else.
The affirmative's edge is `withAlpha(tc.success, 0.28)` rather than
rgba(63,139,123,0.28), which was the dark theme's success frozen at 28%
and wrong in light mode. And undo moves onto the gold hairline: two
coloured buttons and a grey one read as three unrelated controls.

Undo's glyph is a circular arrow rather than the angular undo hook — it
brings the previous card round again, where the hook meant revert an
edit. Still routed through `directionalIcon`, which passes an unmirrored
name through: a circle has no reading direction to flip, and sending
every Ionicon through it is what makes the ones that do need mirroring
impossible to forget.

HERO_PLATE 100 → 86 for the chip's new row; iPhone SE gains the rest as
card (0.701 → 0.733).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Drop the hero poster, centre the deck, colour the card by its band
entry.content:
Drop the hero poster, centre the deck, colour the card by its band

The poster was the single full-colour object on a screen whose subject
is one word, so the eye landed on it first on every open. It is gone.
The backdrop wash still says which film this is — from behind the type
rather than beside it — and the title and its meta line stay where they
were.

Two things follow. The hero block was the poster's height because the
poster was the tallest thing in it; it is now the title's (HERO_PLATE
100 → 76). And the deck centres in what the column has left instead of
sitting at the top with the slack pooling underneath, which read as the
card hanging off the hero rather than being the point of the screen. The
poster's 24pt lands on the SE as a bigger card (scale 0.701 → 0.755) and
on larger phones as air either side of the deck, since those are clamped
at 1 already.

The word's translation now takes the band's colour, the one the chip
above it already wears and the one the target word is highlighted in
below. Three marks on one card that all mean "this word is C1" — in
three colours they read as three unrelated decorations, and the level
stops being a fact the card states and becomes a badge in a corner.
"Same as English" still opts out: that line is a statement about the
word rather than a translation of it, so its override sits after the
band colour and wins.

The poster zoom modal went with the poster — it was the only thing
reaching it.

entry.title: Revert the dim and vignette on MovieDetail
entry.content:
Revert the dim and vignette on MovieDetail

Reverts 6fd1c69 and e5d40f2. The word deck's focus wash is gone by
request: no FocusWash, no ambient strength, and Vignette goes back to
its single fixed reach.

Both commits rather than just the screen. The shared `theme/dim` and
SearchDimOverlay's refactor onto it only existed because a second
receding surface had arrived — with that surface gone there is one
caller again, so the extraction is a layer of indirection over a single
use. SearchDimOverlay owns its two alphas directly, exactly as it did
before, and its test pins them there again.

The search overlay's own dim is untouched and still works: it was never
part of this.
